                                                                                       Researchers have found sRPE methodology to be an in-
                                                                                   expensive, efficient, and reliable way to measure internal TL in
                                                                                   place of expensive and more invasive HR monitoring (7,15,21).
                                                                                   There are moderately strong relationships between objective and
                                                                                   subjective measurements of internal load in Canadian football
                                                                                   (7), basketball (30), and soccer (21) players with correlation
                                                                                   coefficients ranging between 0.68 and 0.85. The results from this
                                                                                   study found a slightly lower correlation coefficient in our NCAA
                                                                                   DII American football players (r 5 0.62), but still in reasonable
                                                                                   agreement with previous studies. A possible explanation for the
                                                                                   lower correlation coefficient documented in this study is that the
                                                                                   sRPE load ratings included other physiological stressors
                                                                                   (i.e., ambient environment, and psychological stress) imposed on
                                                                                   the athletes during preseason camp that might not have been
                                                                                   captured in previous studies that were observed over an entire
                                                                                   football season (7) and over multiple weeks of preseason camp
                                                                                   (22). In addition, to further explain the differences in correlations
                                                                                   between sports, there are specific factors to the sport of football
                                                                                   that could influence players perception of load. First, football
                                                                                   players train with large amounts of protective equipment and the
                                                                                   added equipment could explain the difference between this study
                                                                                   and other outdoor field sports such as soccer (9). In addition, it is
                                                                                   possible that the intense collisions in football could influence
                                                                                   player perception of the load experienced compared with other
                                                                                   sports such as basketball (7,40).
                                                                                       In addition to assessing relationships between objective and
                                                                                   subjective assessments of internal TL in athletes, in this study, we
                                                                                   examined the main FBC and SCC’s ability to quantify internal TL
                                                                                   in athletes. Similar studies, seeking to investigate whether sport
                                                                                   coaches can accurately determine athletes internal load, have
                                                                                   been performed in soccer (4), volleyball (35), and basketball (28),
                                                                                   but not with American FBCs. The results from this study highlight
                                                                                   that the FBC was more accurate in observing the athletes’ internal
                                                                                   TL with a moderate correlation (r 5 0.68). This moderately
                                                                                   strong correlation aligns with previous studies (r 5 0.70–0.84),
                                                                                   which have examined coaches’ observed TL and athletes’ TL with

code.description: Source code to execute. Use console.log (JS/TS), print (Python/Ruby/Perl/R), echo (Shell), echo (PHP), fmt.Println (Go), IO.puts (Elixir), or Console.WriteLine (C#) to output a summary to context.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs (which is the right layer for this policy). Pass an explicit value for long-running builds (Gradle/Maven/SBT).

background.description: Keep process running after timeout (for servers/daemons). Returns partial output without killing the process. IMPORTANT: Do NOT add setTimeout/self-close timers in background scripts — the process must stay alive until the timeout detaches it. For server+fetch patterns, prefer putting both server and fetch in ONE ctx_execute call instead of using background.

cwd.description: Optional working directory for shell commands. Non-shell languages still execute from their sandbox temp directory.

intent.description:
What you're looking for in the output. When provided and output is large (>5KB), indexes output into knowledge base and returns section titles + previews — not full content. Use ctx_search(queries: [...]) to retrieve specific sections. Example: 'failing tests', 'HTTP 500 errors'.

TIP: Use specific technical terms, not just concepts. Check 'Searchable terms' in the response for available vocabulary.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file
entries.description:
Read a file into a sandboxed FILE_CONTENT variable and run code over it. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation — the file bytes stay in the sandbox.

Think-in-Code applied to file-level analysis: Reading the whole file means every byte enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. Running code over it here lets you keep the raw bytes out and only the derived answer in. Same principle as ctx_execute, scoped to one named file via the FILE_CONTENT variable.

WHEN:
  - You want to KNOW SOMETHING ABOUT a file (line count, matches of a pattern, parsed structure, statistical aggregate) without needing to SEE all of it
  - The file is structured (CSV, JSON, log, code) and a code-level derivation is cheaper than reading verbatim

WHEN NOT:

  - The file is small AND you will consume all of it for understanding/editing — Read directly

                                                                                                                                                                                 Testing procedures


                                                                                                                                                                                        Participants completed a 2-day experimental protocol separated by 48 h. The

                                                                                                                                                                                 first testing session was used for anthropometric assessments, medical examinations and

                                                                                                                                                                                 taking resting blood samples. For this, participants arrived at the laboratory in a well-

                                                                                                                                                                                 rested condition and a fasted state. During the second testing session, each participant

                                                                                                                                                                                 performed a 20 m sprint test, a vertical jump test (CMJ), a progressive loading test and a

                                                                                                                                                                                 fatigue test in the SQ exercise. Before the physical performance assessment, all


                                                                                                                                                                                                                             11
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               Page 12 of 47




                                                                                                                                                                                 participants carried out a general standardized warm-up consisting of 5 min of running




                         Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by OHIO STATE UNIVERSITY on 05/07/20
                                                                                                                                                                                 at a self-selected intensity, 5 min of joint mobilization exercises, followed by 3 sets of

                                                                                                                                                                                 progressively faster 30 m running accelerations. Exactly the same testing protocol was

                                                                                                                                                                                 carried out during both Pre and Post testing sessions. Testing sessions were performed

                                                                                                                                                                                 in the same laboratory at the same venue and the same time of day (±1 h) for each

                                                                                                                                                                                 participant, under the same environmental conditions (~21 °C and ~60 % humidity). At

                                                                                                                                                                                 least three experienced researchers supervised the testing sessions to ensure correct and

                                                                                                                                                                                 consistent techniques were used during all tests. Strong verbal encouragement was

                                                                                                                                                                                 provided during all tests to motivate participants to give a maximal effort.




                                                                                                                                                                                 Running sprint test




For personal use only. This Just-IN manuscript is the accepted manuscript prior to copy editing and page composition. It may differ from the final official version of record.
                                                                                                                                                                                        Participants carried out two maximal 20-m running sprints (3-min rest) on a

                                                                                                                                                                                 synthetic indoor running track and the best of both attempts was kept for analysis. The

                                                                                                                                                                                 specific warm-up protocol consisted of one 0-40 m sprint at 80% effort, two 0-30 m

                                                                                                                                                                                 sprints at 90% effort and one 0-20 m sprint at maximal effort. Photocell timing gates

                                                                                                                                                                                 (Wireless training timer, Microgate, Bolzano, Italy) were placed at 0, 10 and 20 m so

                                                                                                                                                                                 that the times to cover 0-10 m (T10) and 0-20 m (T20) could be determined. A standing

                                                                                                                                                                                 start, with the lead-off foot placed 1 m behind the first timing gate was used. The

                                                                                                                                                                                 coefficients of variation (CV) for test-retest reliability for T10 and T20 were 1.8% and

                                                                                                                                                                                 1.0%, respectively. The intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) were 0.90 (95%

                                                                                                                                                                                 confidence interval, CI: 0.78-0.95) for T10, and 0.97 (95% CI: 0.94-0.99) for T20.




                                                                                                                                                                                 Countermovement jump test



                                                                                                                                                                                                                             12
                                                  Page 13 of 47




                                                                                                                                                                                        A CMJ was performed with the participant standing in an upright position on an




                         Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by OHIO STATE UNIVERSITY on 05/07/20
                                                                                                                                                                                 infrared timing system (Optojump System, Microgate, Bolzano, Italy) with hands on the

                                                                                                                                                                                 hips to avoid arm swings. A fast downward movement was immediately followed by a

                                                                                                                                                                                 fast upward vertical movement as high as possible, all in one sequence. Five trials were

                                                                                                                                                                                 completed with a 45 s rest between each trial. The highest and lowest values were

                                                                                                                                                                                 discarded, and the resulting mean value was kept for analysis. The specific warm-up

                                                                                                                                                                                 consisted of 2 sets of 10 repetitions of the squat exercise without extra load (2 min rest),

                                                                                                                                                                                 5 CMJs at progressive intensity (20s rest) and 3 maximal CMJs (30s rest). The CV was

                                                                                                                                                                                 1.6% and the ICC was 0.99 (95% CI: 0.99-1.00).

                                                                                                                                                                                        A detailed description of the SQ testing protocol has been recently provided

                                                                                                                                                                                 elsewhere (Sánchez-Medina et al. 2017). Testing was performed on a Smith machine

                                                                                                                                                                                 (Multipower Fitness Line, Peroga, Murcia, Spain). The participants performed the SQ

                                                                                                                                                                                 from an upright position, descending (eccentric phase) in a continuous motion until the

                                                                                                                                                                                 posterior thighs and calves made contact with each other, then immediately reversed the

                                                                                                                                                                                 motion and ascended back to the starting position. The eccentric phase was performed at

                                                                                                                                                                                 a controlled velocity (~0.50 - 0.60m·s-1), whereas participants were required to always

                                                                                                                                                                                 execute the concentric phase at maximal intended velocity in all repetitions. Verbal

                                                                                                                                                                                 information about movement velocity during eccentric phase was provided after each

                                                                                                                                                                                 repetition in order to maintain the bar velocity within the established range. The specific

                                                                                                                                                                                 warm-up consisted of two sets of eight and six SQ repetitions (3-min rests) with loads

                                                                                                                                                                                 of 20 and 30 kg, respectively. The initial load was set at 30 kg for all participants and

                                                                                                                                                                                 was gradually increased in 10 kg increments until the mean propulsive velocity (MPV)

                                                                                                                                                                                 m·s-1) loads. Interset rests ranged from 3 (light) to 5 min (heavy loads). The exact same

                                                                                                                                                                                 exercise was chosen as training exercise because this type of exercise induce greater

                                                                                                                                                                                 neuromuscular and functional adaptations and lower pain than half- or quarter-squat

                                                                                                                                                                                 after prolonged RT period (Hartmann et al. 2013; Pallares et al. 2019). Training

                                                                                                                                                                                 variables such as relative intensity (70%-85% 1RM), number of sets (three), recovery

                                                                                                                                                                                 performance improvement (Ahtiainen et al. 2003; Kraemer and Ratamess 2005).

                                                                                                                                                                                 However, our results and other previous studies (Hakkinen et al. 1987; Izquierdo et al.

                                                                                                                                                                                 2006) showed significant increments in physical performance without significant

                                                                                                                                                                                 changes in the testosterone-cortisol ratio. Therefore, the use of this biomarker remains

                                                                                                                                                                                 questionable.




                                                                                                                                                                                        Similar to our results, most studies found that RT had no influence on resting

                                                                                                                                                                                 concentrations of GH and IGF-1 hormones (Izquierdo et al. 2006; Kraemer et al. 1999;

                                                                                                                                                                                 Marx et al. 2001), despite the importance assigned to these hormones for tissue




For personal use only. This Just-IN manuscript is the accepted manuscript prior to copy editing and page composition. It may differ from the final official version of record.
                                                                                                                                                                                 remodeling in response to resistance exercise (Kraemer and Ratamess 2005; McCall et

                                                                                                                                                                                 al. 1999). In contrast, other studies showed increments in IGF-1 after RT with high

                                                                                                                                                                                 volumes (Koziris et al. 1999; Marx et al. 2001), suggesting that this factor is relevant

                                                                                                                                                                                 for chronic adaptations in this hormone (Kraemer and Ratamess 2005). However, in the

                                                                                                                                                                                 present study, although VL30% performed more than half of the repetitions performed

                                                                                                                                                                                 by VL10%, no significant or practical changes were observed in either experimental

                                                                                                                                                                                 group. Therefore, it appears that further studies are necessary to clarify the influence of

                                                                                                                                                                                 different variables such as relative intensity and volume on chronic changes in resting

                                                                                                                                                                                 IGF-1 concentration.




                                                                                                                                                                                 Conclusions


                                                                                                                                                                                 The main findings of the current study were the following:
                                                                                                                                                                                                                              30
                                                  Page 31 of 47




                                                                                                                                                                                    The VL10% group showed similar or even greater percentage of changes in muscle




                         Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by OHIO STATE UNIVERSITY on 05/07/20
                                                                                                                                                                                     strength and endurance, jump and sprint performance compared to VL30%.

                                                                                                                                                                                    For VL10%, gains in muscle strength were accompanied by a slightly increase in

                                                                                                                                                                                     neural activation of the agonist musculature involved in the SQ exercise (VLA and

                                                                                                                                                                                     VME), whereas the EMG activity remained unchanged for VL30%.

                                                                                                                                                                                    The VL30% group showed greater increments in TnT than VL10%. In addition,

                                                                                                                                                                                     although no significant differences between experimental groups were observed in

                                                                                                                                                                                     resting hormonal concentration, VL30% showed higher percentage increments in

                                                                                                                                                                                     different anabolic hormones (GH and IGF-1) than VL10%.

                                                                                                                                                                                    For load magnitudes of 70-85% 1RM, and executing each repetition at maximal

                                                                                                                                                                                     intended velocity, a curvilinear relationship between percentage VL in the set and

                                                                                                                                                                                     changes in strength variables and CMJ performance was observed, with 10% and




For personal use only. This Just-IN manuscript is the accepted manuscript prior to copy editing and page composition. It may differ from the final official version of record.
                                                                                                                                                                                     20% VL showing greater percentage changes compared to 30% and 40% VL,

                                                                                                                                                                                     respectively. A linear relationship was found between changes in T20 and VL in the

                                                                                                                                                                                     set.




                                                                                                                                                                                 Practical applications


                                                                                                                                                                                 The results of the current study will allow us to improve knowledge about the design

                                                                                                                                                                                 and quantification of degree of fatigue during RT, as well as to determine the effect of a

                                                                                                                                                                                 given training load. Monitoring the VL in the set against the same range of relative

                                                                                                                                                                                 loads provides valid, accurate and objective information for determining the degree of

                                                                                                                                                                                 fatigue that will maximize gains in physical performance. As shown in this study, the

                                                                                                                                                                                 VL experienced during each training set directly influences functional, neural and

                                                                                                                                                                                 probably structural adaptations. Thus, our results appear to confirm the hypothesis that


                                                                                                                                                                                                                            31
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Page 32 of 47




                                                                                                                                                                                 reaching VL in the set higher than 20% in the SQ exercise produces lower gains in




                         Appl. Physiol. Nutr. Metab. Downloaded from www.nrcresearchpress.com by OHIO STATE UNIVERSITY on 05/07/20
                                                                                                                                                                                 neuromuscular performance. However, the present study also suggests that VL in the set

                                                                                                                                                                                 as low as 10% (2-4 repetitions) may be similar to or even more beneficial than higher

                                                                                                                                                                                 levels of VL for obtaining increments in physical performance. These findings are of

                                                                                                                                                                                 great practical relevance for those athletes aiming to improve their ability to apply force

                                                                                                                                                                                 over short time periods without an excessive degree of fatigue that could interfere with

                                                                                                                                                                                 other specific technical-tactical skills, and avoiding excessive muscle hypertrophy that

                                                                                                                                                                                 could produce an increase in body weight that would negatively affect performance.

{
  "id": "Q65",
  "sourceFile": "Therapeutic potential for cannabinoids in sports medicine - Current literature review.pdf",
  "decision": "INCLUDE",
  "exclusionReason": "",
  "degradedReason": "",
  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Therapeutic Potential for Cannabinoids in Sports Medicine: Current Literature Review' (Naik and Trojian, Current Sports Medicine Reports) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
  "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
  "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Brain Health & Psychology"],
  "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training"],
  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
  "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review by Naik and Trojian of cannabidiol (CBD) and THC for common sports medicine problems: osteoarthritis, concussion, chronic pain, sports performance anxiety, cardiovascular effects and adverse effects. The authors draw mainly on animal, in vitro and non-sport studies, and state that high-quality human trials in sports medicine are lacking. They do not recommend CBD for concussion at this time.",
  "screeningLimitations": "No search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal is described, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked for completeness. The performance and anxiety points rest on resting cardiovascular and general anxiety studies, and the authors state that no CBD study has examined sports performance anxiety. The legal and market section reflects 2020-2021 sources.",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as evidence that CBD treats osteoarthritis, concussion or pain in athletes, when the cited support is mostly preclinical and the authors do not recommend CBD for concussion.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2021,
    "citation": "Naik H, Trojian TH. Therapeutic Potential for Cannabinoids in Sports Medicine: Current Literature Review. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2021;20(7):345-350.",
    "doi": "10.1249/jsr.0000000000000858",
    "abstract": "The review compares cannabidiol and delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol through the endocannabinoid system and summarizes their theoretical benefits and current U.S. legal status for common sports medicine conditions, to help clinicians answer questions from athletes and active patients.",
    "tldr": "This is a clinician guide rather than trial evidence. Cannabidiol shows anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects in animal and in vitro work, but human sports medicine trials are lacking. The authors do not recommend CBD for concussion and do not recommend medical marijuana containing THC.",
    "methods": "Narrative literature review. The article does not describe a search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal.",
    "findings": "Covers CB1, CB2, TRPV1, serotonin and GPR55 pharmacology. Reports animal and in vitro evidence of pain and inflammation relief and possible joint protection in osteoarthritis, with limited human trials. For concussion, the authors state that trials do not exist and they do not recommend use. Anxiolytic effects are reported under stress, with inconsistent results at low stress and increased anxiety at 600 mg in one high-paranoia group. Cardiovascular findings are inconsistent, and the cited studies were done at rest rather than during exercise.",
    "limitations": "The review is narrative and unsystematic, so the choice of evidence is not transparent. Most mechanistic and chronic pain support is preclinical. The authors state that human trials, dosing, safety and long-term effects remain unresolved in sports medicine. Legal and market content is U.S.-specific and reflects 2020-2021 sources.",
    "practicalImplications": "Expect athletes and active patients to ask about CBD for osteoarthritis, pain, concussion and pre-competition anxiety. Explain that the evidence is mostly animal or in vitro, that CBD is not recommended for concussion, and that the authors advise against medical marijuana containing THC because nonprescription THC products are not federally legal. Pre-competition CBD dosing should not be based on this review.",
    "athleteDev": "The review contains no performance outcome data in athletes. Its cardiovascular and anxiety evidence is resting or non-sport based, and the authors state that CBD has not been studied for sports performance anxiety. It cannot support a performance or pre-competition dosing recommendation.",
    "rtp": "This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It contains no trials of cannabinoids for concussion or injury recovery, and the authors do not recommend CBD for concussion at this time."
  }
}

{
  "id": "Q66",
  "sourceFile": "Training Impulse and Session Ratings of Perceived Exertion as Perceived by Athletes and Observed by Coaches During Preseason Football Camp.pdf",
  "decision": "INCLUDE",
  "exclusionReason": "",
  "degradedReason": "",
  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Training Impulse and Session Ratings of Perceived Exertion as Perceived by Athletes and Observed by Coaches During Preseason Football Camp' (Smith-Hale et al., J Strength Cond Res) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",
  "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
  "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance", "Recovery & Readiness"],
  "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
  "sports": ["American Football"],
  "populations": ["Collegiate"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Prospective study of 24 NCAA Division II football athletes (6 first-year, 18 returning) and 2 coaches over the first 6 days of preseason camp. It compares heart-rate training impulse (Edwards TRIMP, from chest-strap monitors) with session RPE rated by athletes and by the football and strength and conditioning coaches. The authors report significant but low-to-moderate correlations (athletes r = 0.62, football coach r = 0.68, strength and conditioning coach r = 0.49), stronger in first-year athletes, and conclude the measures are not interchangeable.",
  "screeningLimitations": "Agreement was assessed with correlations only, not bias or limits of agreement. The sample is small, drawn from one team, and unbalanced (6 first-year and 18 returning athletes), and estimated maximal heart rate (220 minus age) was used for most athletes. Recovery associations are small and were tested within subgroups.",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read these correlations as showing that coach observation or athlete ratings can replace heart-rate monitoring. The authors say the measures are not interchangeable and present the work as a preliminary study.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2025,
    "citation": "Smith-Hale V, Mendoza R, Vargo C, Schoen M, Jimenez L, VanSumeren M, et al. Training Impulse and Session Ratings of Perceived Exertion as Perceived by Athletes and Observed by Coaches During Preseason Football Camp. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025.",
    "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000005169",
    "abstract": "Compared heart-rate training impulse with session RPE from athletes, a football coach and a strength and conditioning coach during the first six practices of preseason camp in collegiate American football players, and examined first-year versus returning athletes and recovery measures.",
    "tldr": "In one Division II football team's first six camp practices, athlete and coach ratings of session load tracked heart-rate load only moderately. Use ratings alongside heart-rate data, not as a substitute for it.",
    "methods": "Prospective study during the first six official practices of preseason camp. Athletes wore chest-strap heart-rate monitors to calculate TRIMP and rated each session on the CR10 session RPE scale. The football and strength and conditioning coaches rated each athlete. Heart rate variability and resting heart rate were measured before practice. Pearson correlations and Mann-Whitney U tests were used.",
    "findings": "Across 139 observations, session loads correlated significantly with Edwards TRIMP: athletes r = 0.62, football coach r = 0.68 and strength and conditioning coach r = 0.49. Correlations were stronger in first-year athletes. First-year athletes had a higher heart-rate load than returning athletes (median 780 vs 697), but their own ratings did not differ (median 780 vs 735). Heart rate variability was inversely related to load (r = -0.29 for Edwards TRIMP) and resting heart rate positively related (r = 0.22), both small.",
    "limitations": "Small, unbalanced sample of 24 athletes and 2 coaches from one team over six practices. Maximal heart rate was estimated for most athletes, which may have lowered TRIMP scores. The strength and conditioning coach correlation is 0.49 in the abstract and results but 0.41 in the Discussion, and the Figure 3 caption reverses the first-year and returning group sizes. Recovery relationships are small. The study had no outside funding and was not endorsed by NSCA.",
    "practicalImplications": "Ratings and heart-rate load agree only moderately, so session RPE from athletes or coaches should not replace heart-rate monitoring. The authors suggest that both kinds of measure add unique information, and that coaches and athletes may align their ratings more closely with feedback on heart rate.",
    "athleteDev": "During preseason camp, athlete and football coach ratings tracked heart-rate load reasonably well, though with low-to-moderate agreement. The strength and conditioning coach's ratings agreed least, which suggests that coach needs better information on cumulative load in field practices.",
    "rtp": "The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It examined collegiate athletes in preseason practice and did not study injured or returning athletes or return-to-play decisions."
  }
}

  "decision": "INCLUDE",

  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Velocity-based resistance training: Impact of velocity loss in the set on neuromuscular performance and hormonal response' (Rodriguez-Rosell et al., Appl Physiol Nutr Metab accepted manuscript) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Randomized Controlled Trial",
  "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
  "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
  "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching"],
  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
  "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Randomized two-group study of 25 young healthy men (10% velocity loss per set, n = 12; 30% velocity loss, n = 13) who trained twice weekly for 8 weeks with velocity-based full-squat sets at 70-85% 1RM. The authors report similar strength and fatigue-test gains in both groups, larger percentage gains in countermovement jump and 10 m and 20 m sprint time in the 10% group despite about half the repetitions, and a larger rise in troponin T in the 30% group. Between-group differences in strength were not significant.",
  "screeningLimitations": "Small sample of physically active sport science students, not elite athletes, with two training arms and no untrained control. Only the full squat was trained and tested, and between-group differences in jump and strength were small. The 1RM was estimated from bar velocity rather than measured directly. Most hormone and EMG changes were not significant, and the abstract's EMG statement is stronger than the results.",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 10% velocity-loss result as proof that low-fatigue sets suit athletes in general. This was an 8-week study in active students, and the between-group strength and jump differences were not significant.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2020,
    "citation": "Rodríguez-Rosell D, Yáñez-García JM, Mora-Custodio R, Pareja-Blanco F, Ravelo-García AG, Ribas-Serna J, et al. Velocity-based resistance training: Impact of velocity loss in the set on neuromuscular performance and hormonal response. Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism. 2020.",
    "doi": "10.1139/apnm-2019-0829",
    "abstract": "Compared 10% and 30% velocity loss per set in an 8-week full-squat velocity-based program in 25 young men, measuring strength, jump, sprint, fatigue, knee extensor EMG and resting hormones.",
    "tldr": "In physically active men, sets stopped at 10% velocity loss produced strength and jump gains similar to sets at 30%, with under half the repetitions. Sprint times improved more in the 10% group, and only the 30% group showed a larger rise in troponin T.",
    "methods": "Randomized two-group, 8-week study. Participants were matched on estimated 1RM and randomly assigned. Both groups trained the full squat at 70-85% 1RM, three sets per session, twice weekly, with each set ended at 10% or 30% velocity loss. Pre and post tests included a 20 m sprint, countermovement jump, a progressive loading test with estimated 1RM, a fatigue test, knee extensor EMG and resting blood hormones.",
    "findings": "Compliance was 100%. Both groups improved estimated 1RM (VL10% +17.9%, VL30% +14.9%) and fatigue-test repetitions (+74.8% and +73.2%). Countermovement jump rose 9.2% in the 10% group and 5.4% in the 30% group, with a small between-group effect (0.23) that was not significant. Sprint times for 10 m and 20 m improved only in the 10% group (about -1.5% to -1.6%), with a significant time-by-group interaction. EMG changes were not significant in either group. Troponin T rose 59.9% (10%) and 128.4% (30%), a significant within-group change in both groups and a larger rise in the 30% group. No other resting hormone changed significantly.",
    "limitations": "1RM was estimated from bar velocity rather than measured. Only 25 men completed the study, and there was no untrained control group. The abstract says only the 10% group showed EMG increments, but the Results report no significant EMG change in either group. The Results give the 10% group repetition SD as 12.0 in one place and 2.0 in another. The year 2020 is taken from the Crossref record; the PDF is an accepted manuscript that prints only a download stamp, with no volume, issue or pages.",
    "practicalImplications": "Stopping sets at a set velocity loss is a practical way to control fatigue in a 70-85% 1RM squat program. Sets ended at 10% loss gave strength and fatigue gains similar to 30% loss with fewer repetitions, so shorter sets may suit programs focused on jump and sprint performance. This needs confirmation in trained athletes.",
    "athleteDev": "In this sample of active men, a 10% velocity-loss set (about 2 to 4 repetitions) gave strength and fatigue-test gains similar to a 30% set, with larger sprint and jump percentage gains and about half the repetitions. Coaches could use velocity loss as a set-ending rule, but the study was short, used non-elite men, and did not measure sport performance.",
    "rtp": "The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested injury-free men in a laboratory training block and included no injured or rehabilitating participants."
  }
}

      Derivatives: Barbell and System
      Velocity Comparisons

          Abstract
          Suchomel, TJ, Kissick, CR, Techmanski, BS, Mann, JB, and Comfort, P. Velocity-based training with weightlifting derivatives:
          Barbell and system velocity comparisons. J Strength Cond Res 39(2): 135–146, 2025—The aim of this study was to examine the
          differences in barbell and system (i.e., subject + load) velocity during weightlifting derivatives performed across a spectrum of
          relative loads. 14 resistance-trained men participated in 6 testing sessions, which included 1 repetition maximum hang power clean
          (HPC) testing and individual jump shrug (JS), hang high pull (HHP), HPC, hang clean pull (HCP), and countermovement shrug (CMS)
          sessions. The order of the exercise testing sessions was randomized and required the subjects to perform either JS, HHP, HPC,
          HCP, or CMS repetitions while standing on a force platform with a linear position transducer attached to the barbell. The JS and
          HHP were performed with 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100% of their 1 repetition maximum HPC, HPC with 20, 40, 60, and 80% 1RM, and
          the HCP and CMS performed with 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, and 140% 1RM. Mean and peak barbell and system velocities were
          determined across all exercises and loads using either 2 3 5, 2 3 4, or 2 3 7 repeated measures ANOVA depending on the number
          of loads performed. Significantly (p , 0.001) and meaningfully (g $ 1.49) greater mean and peak barbell velocities existed at every
          exercise and load combination compared with the mean and peak system velocities produced. Barbell and system velocity are
          distinct characteristics that should not be substituted for one another. Owing to the characteristics of the transition phase, mean
          barbell and system velocity may not provide strength and conditioning practitioners with meaningful information related to load
          prescription.
          Key Words: jump shrug, hang high pull, hang power clean, hang pull, countermovement shrug, Olympic weightlifting

  "id": "Q68",
  "sourceFile": "Velocity-Based Training With Weightlifting Derivatives - Barbell and System Velocity Comparisons.pdf",
  "decision": "INCLUDE",
  "exclusionReason": "",
  "degradedReason": "",
  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Velocity-Based Training With Weightlifting Derivatives: Barbell and System Velocity Comparisons' (Suchomel et al., J Strength Cond Res) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",
  "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
  "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance"],
  "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
  "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Repeated-measures study in 14 resistance-trained men who were not competitive weightlifters. Each performed single repetitions of the jump shrug, hang high pull, hang power clean, hang clean pull and countermovement shrug across 4 to 7 loads (20% to 140% of hang power clean 1RM), measured with a barbell linear position transducer and a force platform. The authors report that mean and peak barbell velocities were significantly greater than system velocities at every exercise and load (p < 0.001, Hedges g at least 1.49), and conclude the two measures should not be substituted for one another.",
  "screeningLimitations": "Only single repetitions were tested, not sets, and several loads (20% to 40% of hang power clean 1RM) are lighter than these lifts are usually prescribed. The sample was 14 men who were not competitive weightlifters, so generalization to women, weightlifters or other groups is limited. System velocity CVs exceeded 10% at some light loads (for example, 11.7% for the jump shrug at 20%).",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the barbell-system gap as a reason to treat the two velocity measures as interchangeable, or to set loads for these pulls from mean barbell velocity zones built for other lifts. The authors say the measures are distinct and that mean velocity may not guide load prescription for these pulls.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2025,
    "citation": "Suchomel TJ, Kissick CR, Techmanski BS, Mann JB, Comfort P. Velocity-Based Training With Weightlifting Derivatives: Barbell and System Velocity Comparisons. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025;39(2):135-146.",
    "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000004962",
    "abstract": "Compared mean and peak barbell velocity with system velocity (athlete plus load) during five weightlifting derivatives across a range of relative loads in 14 resistance-trained men, using force platforms and linear position transducers.",
    "tldr": "In resistance-trained men, barbell velocity was consistently and substantially higher than system velocity across five weightlifting pulls and every load tested. Treat the two as different measures, and do not swap one for the other when setting loads.",
    "methods": "Repeated-measures design. Participants completed six sessions over about two weeks, starting with a 1RM hang power clean test, then exercise sessions in randomized order. Single repetitions were performed at 20% to 100% (jump shrug and hang high pull), 20% to 80% (hang power clean), and 20% to 140% (hang clean pull and countermovement shrug) of hang power clean 1RM. Barbell velocity came from a linear position transducer and system velocity from force-platform integration. Reliability was assessed with ICC and CV, and differences with repeated-measures ANOVA and Hedges g.",
    "findings": "Mean and peak barbell velocity exceeded system velocity at every exercise and load (p < 0.001, Hedges g at least 1.49). For example, the hang power clean at 20% gave mean barbell velocity 1.46 m/s against system velocity 0.62 m/s. Most system velocities were below 1.00 m/s, except the jump shrug at 20% to 60%. Reliability was mostly good to excellent for both measures (ICCs mostly 0.84 to 0.99), with system velocity CVs above 10% at some light loads.",
    "limitations": "Single repetitions rather than sets, some loads lighter than typical prescription, and a small sample of resistance-trained men who were not competitive weightlifters. System velocity was less reliable at light loads. The authors note that subject height and limb length may affect barbell velocity, and call for research across sets and populations.",
    "practicalImplications": "Use peak velocity to characterize these weightlifting derivatives. Barbell velocity may matter most for weightlifters, while system velocity may be more relevant for non-weightlifters who use derivatives in training. Because the transition phase limits how well mean velocity reflects load, it should not be the main basis for load prescription in these pulls.",
    "athleteDev": "For exercise and load selection, use peak velocity to characterize the pulling derivatives. Barbell velocity may guide weightlifters, and system velocity may be more relevant for non-weightlifters. Mean velocity may be a poor basis for load prescription in these lifts.",
    "rtp": "The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested single repetitions of pulling lifts in a lab with resistance-trained men and did not include injured athletes or return-to-play testing."
  }
}

  "id": "Q69",
  "sourceFile": "Vitamin C supplementation and athletic performance - A review.pdf",
  "decision": "INCLUDE",
  "exclusionReason": "",
  "degradedReason": "",
  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Vitamin C Supplementation and Athletic Performance: A Review' (Rogers, Lawlor and Moeller, Current Sports Medicine Reports) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
  "primaryDomain": "Nutrition & Hydration",
  "domains": ["Nutrition & Hydration", "Training & Performance", "Recovery & Readiness"],
  "audiences": ["Nutrition", "Performance", "Coaching"],
  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
  "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Review of 14 double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trials of supraphysiologic vitamin C in athletes and active adults, identified by a PubMed search of 2012 to 2022 (97 articles screened). Most trials combined vitamin C with vitamin E or another antioxidant. The authors report that three trials found lower muscle damage markers with vitamin C-containing supplements, while the other 11 found neutral or negative effects on muscle damage, performance, soreness or training adaptation.",
  "screeningLimitations": "The review is a single PubMed search with a narrow keyword set and no meta-analysis or formal quality grading. Most of the 14 trials had fewer than 60 participants, and most combined vitamin C with other antioxidants, so vitamin C effects cannot be separated. Populations are mixed, from elderly men and students to elite taekwondo athletes.",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as a blanket ban on vitamin C for all athletes, when most trials used vitamin C with vitamin E, the sample sizes were small, and the recommendation rests on a mixed set of studies.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2023,
    "citation": "Rogers DR, Lawlor DJ, Moeller JL. Vitamin C Supplementation and Athletic Performance: A Review. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2023;22(7):255-259.",
    "doi": "10.1249/jsr.0000000000001083",
    "abstract": "Reviews 14 randomized placebo-controlled trials of high-dose vitamin C in athletes and active people, most combined with other antioxidants, on muscle damage, performance and training adaptation.",
    "tldr": "Across 14 placebo-controlled trials, high-dose vitamin C showed no consistent benefit for performance or soreness, and some trials reported blunted training adaptations when taken with vitamin E. The authors advise against long-term high-dose vitamin C and recommend antioxidants from a nutrient-rich diet.",
    "methods": "PubMed search for 2012 to 2022 using the terms vitamin C, ascorbic acid, athlete and performance, yielding 97 articles. Inclusion required a double-blind placebo-controlled randomized trial of supraphysiologic vitamin C (alone or mixed) and an exercise performance or muscle damage outcome. Fourteen trials were included. No pooled analysis was done.",
    "findings": "Three trials (Askari 2012; Chou 2018; Gillam 2022) reported lower muscle damage markers, such as creatine kinase or myoglobin, with vitamin C plus quercetin or vitamin E. The other trials found no benefit for performance, soreness or perceived exertion. Long-term trials of vitamin C plus vitamin E found that placebo groups had larger gains in lean mass and muscle thickness in older men and in strength and hypertrophy in recreational weightlifters, and greater mitochondrial markers in endurance-trained adults. A combined antioxidant taken before exercise reduced cycling power output in hyperoxia.",
    "limitations": "Single search and no formal quality appraisal. Most trials co-supplemented vitamin C with vitamin E or other antioxidants, so vitamin C effects cannot be isolated. Sample sizes are small. The table and text disagree on the sample for the 10-week Martinez-Ferran trial (32 vs 12) and on the vitamin E dose in the Paulsen trial (235 vs 325 mg). Populations and doses vary widely.",
    "practicalImplications": "Athletes asking about high-dose vitamin C for performance or recovery should be told the trial evidence is inconsistent, and that the authors advise against long-term high-dose supplementation because it may blunt training adaptations. Diet is the recommended source of antioxidants. Short-term use around competition is less well studied and needs its own assessment.",
    "athleteDev": "For training adaptation, the review points to possible blunting of strength and endurance gains with long-term high-dose vitamin C plus vitamin E, so staff should not recommend it during training blocks. Acute high-dose use has not shown a consistent performance benefit.",
    "rtp": "The review contains no return-to-sport or injury-recovery trials. Three small trials reported lower muscle damage markers after exercise, but they were not injury studies, and the authors do not recommend long-term high-dose use. These findings cannot support rehabilitation or return-to-sport use."
  }
}

    "athleteDev": "For training adaptation, the review points to possible blunting of strength and endurance gains with long-term high-dose vitamin C plus vitamin E, so staff should not recommend it during training blocks. Acute high-dose use has not shown a consistent performance benefit.",

"tldr": "Across 14 placebo-controlled trials, high-dose vitamin C showed no consistent benefit for performance or soreness, and some trials reported blunted training adaptations when taken with vitamin E. "methods": "PubMed search for 2012 to 2022 using the terms vitamin C, ascorbic acid, athlete and performance, yielding 97 articles. {
  "id": "Q70",
  "sourceFile": "Vitamin D for improved bone health and prevention of stress fractures - A review of the literature.pdf",
  "decision": "INCLUDE",
  "exclusionReason": "",

  "doiMissing": false,
  "identityCheck": "PDF title 'Vitamin D for Improved Bone Health and Prevention of Stress Fractures: A Review of the Literature' (Lawley, Syrop and Fredericson, Current Sports Medicine Reports) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
  "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
  "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Nutrition & Hydration"],
  "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Nutrition"],
  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
  "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
  "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of vitamin D status, bone health and stress fractures, drawing on trials, cohort and case-control studies in children, adults, military recruits and some athletes. The authors report a consistent but heterogeneous association between vitamin D status and stress fracture, with a meta-analysis of eight military studies finding lower 25(OH)D in stress fracture cases (mean difference -2.44 ng/mL, 95% CI -4.05 to -0.84). They recommend vitamin D3 to maintain status in athletes at high stress-fracture risk, but say the data do not support a specific dose or target level for athletes.",
  "screeningLimitations": "No search method is described, so the selection of studies cannot be checked. The authors note that placebo-controlled RCTs in athletes are scarce, and most athlete evidence is observational. Many bone-outcome trials were in children, postmenopausal women or older adults, and the stress-fracture meta-analysis used military personnel rather than sport athletes. Vitamin D thresholds differ across organizations and no validated assay is available.",
  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as proof that vitamin D supplementation prevents stress fractures in athletes. The athlete evidence is mainly observational, the authors say no dose or target level is supported for athletes, and the large meta-analysis they cite found no fracture prevention with supplementation in older adults.",
  "paper": {
    "year": 2020,
    "citation": "Lawley R, Syrop IP, Fredericson M. Vitamin D for Improved Bone Health and Prevention of Stress Fractures: A Review of the Literature. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2020;19(6):202-208.",
    "doi": "10.1249/jsr.0000000000000718",
    "abstract": "Reviews vitamin D physiology, status measurement and bone health, then the evidence linking vitamin D status and supplementation with stress fractures in adolescents, military recruits and athletes.",
    "tldr": "Vitamin D status and stress fracture risk appear linked in athletes and recruits, but the studies are heterogeneous and mostly observational. Vitamin D3 is reasonable to maintain status in high-risk athletes, but the review does not set a dose or target level for them.",
    "methods": "Narrative literature review. The article does not describe a search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal.",
    "findings": "Athletes, especially indoor and endurance athletes, often have low 25(OH)D. A meta-analysis of eight military studies (2,634 personnel) found lower 25(OH)D in stress fracture cases. In a Royal Marine cohort, low baseline 25(OH)D was linked to stress fracture risk. In a British Army study, recovery from lower-limb stress fracture took about 10 weeks with sufficient 25(OH)D, 12 with insufficient and 13 with deficient levels. In a Navy trial, calcium plus vitamin D reduced stress fracture incidence by about 20% (no statistics given in the text). Supplementation trials of bone density in children and adults are mixed, and a meta-analysis of 81 RCTs found no clear fracture or BMD benefit in older adults.",
    "limitations": "No search method or quality appraisal is described. Athlete evidence is mostly observational and small. Vitamin D thresholds differ by organization, and the authors note that 25(OH)D may not be the best marker. The review states that the athlete data are not strong enough to set a dose or target.",
    "practicalImplications": "Consider checking vitamin D status in athletes at high stress-fracture risk, such as indoor or endurance athletes, military-type trainees, and those with prior fracture. The authors suggest vitamin D3 supplementation to maintain status in such athletes, with doses of 800 to 2000 IU daily cited from the general literature rather than athlete trials.",
    "athleteDev": "The review does not support a dose or target serum level for athletic performance. It cites Cannell's suggestion that 50 ng/mL may be ideal for performance, but the authors say the athlete data are not strong enough to set a dose or target for bone health.",
    "rtp": "The only recovery data are military: recruits with sufficient 25(OH)D recovered from lower-limb stress fractures faster than those insufficient or deficient. This does not give a return-to-sport protocol, and the review cannot set return-to-play criteria or a dosing plan for an injured athlete."
  }
}

- **Q65**: INCLUDE. Narrative review, title matches. No identity concern.
- **Q66**: INCLUDE. Title matches. Text conflicts: the SCC r is 0.49 in the abstract and results but 0.41 in the Discussion, and the Figure 3 caption swaps the group sizes.
- **Q67**: INCLUDE, coded as RCT. Title matches. The PDF prints no journal year, so 2020 comes from Crossref. The DOI check returned 403, but the Crossref title match is 1.0. Design coding is a judgment call (randomized, but no untrained control).
- **Q68**: INCLUDE. Title matches. No identity concern.
- **Q69**: INCLUDE, coded as Systematic Review / Meta-analysis because a PubMed search is described. The table and text disagree on the Martínez-Ferrán sample (32 vs 12) and the Paulsen vitamin E dose (235 vs 325 mg).
- **Q70**: INCLUDE. Narrative review, title matches. No identity concern.
- **Q71**: INCLUDE. Narrative review, title matches. No identity concern.
- **Q72**: EXCLUDE under (b), confidence medium. The source is the right article, but it reads as a critical commentary on the CISG 5 statement with no structured evidence review. Upgrade to INCLUDE if you classify it as a clinical review.
